data.text:
Named after the tenth governor of North Dakota, the 14,245-ton S.S. John Burke was a Liberty Ship cargo vessel that was built by the Oregon Shipbuilding Company at Portland, Oregon. The ship’s keel was laid on 20 November 1942 and only 33 days later, on December 13, the hull was launched. After fitting out over the next ten days, John Burke was handed over to the US Navy on 23 December, such was the speed with which Liberty Ships were built during World War II. John Burke was approximately 422 feet long and 57 feet wide, had a top speed of 11 knots, and had a crew of 68 officers and men (40 ship crewmembers and 28 from the US Navy’s Armed Guard, assigned to man the ship’s guns). The ship was armed with two 3-inch guns and eight 20-mm guns.

After being handed over to the US Navy, the Navy placed John Burke under charter to the Northland Transportation Company. John Burke transported war materials and made numerous trips between the United States and Pearl Harbor, Hawaii; Australia; Guadalcanal in the Solomon Islands; and New Guinea.

In early December 1944, John Burke left Seattle, Washington, for the island of Guam. Once she arrived there, ammunition was loaded onto the ship for the American invasion of the island of Mindoro in the Philippines. John Burke left Guam with a 100-ship convoy and arrived off the coast of Leyte in the Philippines on the night of 27 December 1944.

On 28 December 1944, 6 Japanese kamikaze aircraft spotted the convoy. One of the pilots chose John Burke as his target and made his final suicide run into the ship. Despite heavy anti-aircraft fire from the convoy, the kamikaze crashed into John Burke, plowing deep into her hull. 

A brief flash of fire emanated from John Burke and was visible to most of the ships in the convoy. Within seconds an enormous fireball erupted as her entire cargo of munitions detonated, instantly destroying the ship and vaporizing the crew of 68 officers and men. 

Several ships that were steaming near John Burke were damaged by the force of the blast and by flying pieces of the disintegrating cargo ship. A massive shock wave rocked the entire convoy so hard that several ships reported that they had been torpedoed. A US Army transport just aft of John Burke was severely damaged by the blast and sank before it could be identified. As the smoke gradually cleared, nearby ships steamed into the area searching for any survivors from John Burke. They didn’t find a trace of either the ship or her men.

The loss of John Burke and her entire crew showed how unbelievably dangerous it was to transport munitions to a war zone during World War II. But if armies are to win wars on land, they need a steady stream of munitions, usually supplied by ships. Incredibly brave men sailed on those ships, knowing that at any moment their lives could suddenly end in one, blinding, flash. For the people on board John Burke, that’s exactly what happened.

SAME DAY EDIT: ANNIVERSAYA SA BARRIO FIESTA 🎉✨

What. A. Night. 💛

Truly a celebration to remember—complete with fun games, jaw-dropping performances, kilig moments, and even fireworks lighting up the sky for our one and only JM Fyang. 

This event wasn’t without its hurdles—extreme traffic from the thunderstorm, unexpected financial difficulties, last-minute confirmation too close to the event date, and even a sudden change of venue. But you know what? Every challenge was worth it because of the love, support, and joy everyone brought to this celebration. 

Special thanks to our hardworking admins and team live who tirelessly set up the venue and made sure everything ran smoothly. Your dedication made this night possible. 

To our generous sponsors and donors, thank you for standing with us, believing in this community, and sharing your resources to make this celebration possible. Your support lit up the event and gave everyone a night to remember. You are an invaluable part of this journey, and we are deeply grateful. 

To everyone who dressed up, showed up and attended the event on-site, and those who tuned in via livestream, you made this celebration shine brighter! 

Big thanks to Mak ni Ali for lending us the beautiful Anniversary video that added so much heart to this celebration. 

Special acknowledgment as well to Ms. Mave of Mang Inasal for gracing the event with her presence and support. And to JMFyang’s powerhouse team — RMs Ms. Nicole Uy & Ms.  Nichole Peña, their beautiful managers Ms. Portia Dimla & Ms. Gidget Dela Cuesta, Ms. Manel Sevidal, and Manila Creative Artists Agency, Ms. Japeth Purog, Ms Aryan Buccat, thank you for your unwavering guidance and support toward JMFyang, we appreciate everything that you do for them. 

Most of all, our deepest gratitude goes to JM and Fyang. This entire AnniverSaya was for YOU — our inspiration, our source of joy, and the reason this fanmily came together. Thank you for taking the time to prepare, for being present with us, and for allowing us to celebrate YOU in the biggest way we could. Every laugh, every cheer, and every firework was in honor of the love and light you bring to our lives.

NEWS UPDATE | The Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) confirmed that no Filipinos were killed in the recent New York bus crash, as verified by New York State Police.

“No one has approached the Consulate for assistance thus far. It provided its hotline number in social media advisories,” the statement reads.

On Saturday, August 23, the Consulate General of the Philippines in New York posted contact information for anyone needing assistance related to the incident.

“For the victims of the accident or their next of kin, the Consulate can be reached at the Assistance-to-Nationals Hotline (917) 294-0196,” the Consulate stated. | via Katrina Manubay
